transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
New York prosecutors are reopening a criminal investigation into an alleged sexual assault
involving students at Cornell University.
A former Cornell student says she was drugged and gang-raped at the school in 2024.
No criminal charges were filed at the time, but two weeks ago, she filed a lawsuit with
new allegations against Cornell and seven male students.
And there's Brian Mann is in Ithaca, New York, near the Cornell campus.
The lawsuit says some of the men who allegedly raped this woman who's identified as Jane
Doe were allowed to write essays in order to lessen or mitigate disciplinary action
by Cornell.
In a statement, Cornell said there were consequential punishments for the men involved, but the
university declined our request for an interview to clarify what all that means.
It's unclear whether any of these men are still students at the university.
The details of the case have shaken the small college community in upstate New York and
drawn condemnation from around the world.
Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York spoke to NPR about the legislative work she has
promoted to address sexual assaults on college campuses.
I do imagine that many campuses have put in place much better policies than they had a
decade ago, but Congress hasn't done its part.
And we just spent two weeks talking about college sports.
Congress should spend at least that time talking about how to make campuses safe for all students.
Everyone's full interview airs today on NPR's All Things Considered.
As public concerns mount over the advancement of artificial intelligence, the Trump administration
is launching a new online government tool powered by AI companies, Grok and Google's
Gemini.
President Trump argues this will streamline some basic paperwork functions.
NPR's Emily Fang reports Trump is continuing to downplay concerns of leaders in the industry
who have called for more regulation.
Housed at the website America.gov, this new AI-powered tool will look like a chat function.
People can pull it up and ask it for information on, say, how to renew a passport or enroll
in Medicaid.
Joe Jebiot, an Airbnb co-founder who helped launch the function, says Elon Musk's AI
chatbot, Grok, and Google's Gemini will power the new tool.
Trump then signed an executive order to integrate all federal services across agencies into
the AI tool.
All of this interface will go right into our great, brilliant super mind.
Trump also argued once again against regulation on AI, saying the U.S. needs to maintain its
technology lead over China.
Emily Fang, NPR News, the White House.
Former special counsel Jack Smith is defending the criminal cases he has brought against
President Trump.
Smith appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee today.
Republicans alleged Smith abused his authority in the course of his probes.
The ex-special counsel accused the president of breaking the law and trying to overturn
the results of the 2020 election, and of allegedly mishandling classified documents.
This is NPR.
A Venezuelan man who was shot by a federal immigration officer nine days ago in Austin,
Texas, was in court today after being charged with assault, among other crimes.
The Justice Department's complaint alleges Wilbur Garces Perez struck an officer with
his vehicle while attempting to evade authorities during a traffic stop.
An attorney for Garces Perez disputes the claim.
On Sunday, she said her client still had a bullet lodged near his spine and needed surgery.
Garces Perez is due back in court tomorrow for a separate hearing on whether he can remain
in the U.S.
Montana is one of three states that's begun early implementation of new Medicaid work requirements
Later this week, the state will begin removing people from the public health insurance program
if they are not in compliance.
Here's Montana Public Radio's Erin Bolton.
Under Medicaid work requirements, people need to be working, volunteering, or going to school.
Montana will start kicking people off the rolls October 1st if they're out of compliance.
Missoula Montana resident Bethany Zulich is going back to school to become a high school
English teacher.
Zulich didn't think she'd have to prove her enrollment until next year, when she was supposed
to be up for renewal.
Then she got a confusing letter.
Some of the letter says that this information is due at my next recertification and some
of it says it's due within 30 days of the letter.
Critics worry people like Zulich will lose coverage because they're confused.
State health officials say that won't happen and they're ready to smoothly roll out the
new requirements.
For NPR News, I'm Erin Bolton in Columbia Falls, Montana.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News.

topics.text: New York prosecutors reopen criminal investigation into alleged sexual assault at Cornell University
Trump administration launches AI-powered government tool using Grok and Google Gemini at America.gov
Former special counsel Jack Smith defends criminal cases against President Trump before Senate Judiciary Committee
Venezuelan man Wilbur Garces Perez charged with assault after being shot by immigration officer in Austin
Montana begins early implementation of Medicaid work requirements, removing non-compliant people from rolls October 1st
